problem: Prior adversarial attacks on VLN/embodied agents either need software access to pixels, or target static classifiers or QA outputs. None optimize physical in-scene object appearance to hijack a language-conditioned multi-step navigation policy that must generalize to unseen instructions and histories.
motivation: Instruction-following assistive robots deployed in uncontrolled environments could be hijacked by a malicious actor who only changes the appearance of an object in the scene. The attack must work without knowing the user's instruction or the agent's prior path, so it has to generalize across language and observation histories.
key_idea: Use a differentiable renderer (PyTorch3D) on MP3D meshes to optimize the texture of a 3D attack object, under an L-inf budget, so that a frozen whitebox VLN agent (HAMT) stops or follows an attacker-defined trajectory after seeing it, generalizing to unseen instruction-trajectory pairs.
insight: Attacks generalize to novel instructions and histories: 75.98% of unseen R2R test episodes stop at the object versus 0.98% unattacked. Rendering multiple steps (attack viewpoint plus the next two) is critical: test SR rises from 4.08 (1 step) to 19.05 (3 steps). More instructions, larger budget and more iterations help. Larger objects (sofa, table) are easier to attack, while mentioning the object in the instruction has no significant effect, consistent with weak object grounding in VLN agents.
method: Attack instance construction: choose an attack viewpoint and MP3D object (chair, cabinet, table, plant, sofa, TV monitor, covering >=40% of a sub-image) with >=5 training episodes through it; the attack trajectory is a shortest path to a point >=3 m from the original goal.

Differentiable panoramic rendering: PyTorch3D renders the attack viewpoint and the next two steps, only for sub-images containing the object, with a face mask D so gradients reach only the object's texture atlas.

Loss: cross-entropy of the frozen HAMT agent following the attack trajectory (then STOP), conditioned on guide trajectory, instruction and rendered observations, averaged over training episodes with different instructions and histories.

PGD-style update: Adam (lr 1e-2) on the texture with the change limited to L-inf epsilon=0.3 and colors clamped to [0,1]; 300 iterations (600 for RxR), batch 16, best checkpoint chosen by validation nDTW to the attack trajectory.
Single-step stop attack: the empty attack trajectory supervises STOP at the attack viewpoint.

Evaluation protocol: force the agent along the guide trajectory to the attack viewpoint, then let it run freely in the attacked environment. Splits are Train, Validation (both from train episodes) and Test (val-seen episodes), measured against the attack trajectory and against the original goal.

setting.backbone: HAMT (frozen, pretrained weights from the authors) as the victim; the attack is an optimized object texture
setting.training_data: Attack textures are optimized per instance on R2R-train / RxR-train-guide episodes through the attack viewpoint (about 5+ episodes, 80/20 train/val split); the VLN model is not trained
setting.observation: Panoramic RGB rendered from textured MP3D meshes (36 sub-images) plus the instruction
setting.simulator: MP3D meshes with PyTorch3D differentiable rendering (Matterport3D)
setting.privileged: Whitebox access to the VLN model weights and the target environment mesh; attack object and viewpoint chosen using the dataset

numbers_note: The paper is an attack study, so these numbers measure attack effectiveness on HAMT rather than navigation SOTA. The unattacked baseline HAMT on full val-seen with rendered images is SR 69.64 / nDTW 72.16 (R2R) and SR 53.00 / nDTW 59.13 (RxR); with real images, SR 75.61 / nDTW 78.33 (R2R) and SR 59.37 / nDTW 65.41 (RxR).
results: Stop attacks halt HAMT immediately in 75.98% of unseen R2R test episodes (versus 0.98% unattacked). Trajectory attacks raise arrival at the attacker's target from 3.66% to 21.61% SR. They also cut R2R SR on the original instructions from 82.42 to 53.85, and RxR from 59.06 to 25.59. Effects are weaker on RxR for stopping (25.20 vs 14.17) but large in OSR (78.74).
limitations: Whitebox setting only, needing per-instance texture optimization with heavy differentiable-rendering cost (40-90 minutes per attack on an A40); no blackbox attack.
Only simulated, rendered MP3D scenes and one victim model (HAMT); no physical or real-world deployability is tested, and there is a rendering domain gap (about 6-7 SR points).
Attacks are much weaker on RxR, and trajectory-following success on unseen episodes is modest (about 20% SR).
compares_to: Unattacked HAMT in rendered environments (no other baseline attacks)
